clue.text: Derby's filly, kicking out every second, is a lure

indicators.note: kicking out every second letter of these words leaves the first, third, fifth and so on

explanation.surface: A racing report: a young mare at Derby, lashing out, is the attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kicking out every second' removes letters 2, 4, 6... of DERBYSFILLY, keeping D, R, Y, F, L, Y. 'is a' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: An angler's dry fly is an artificial fly floated on the water to tempt trout, so it is a kind of bait.

clue.text: Bouncer initially tests England's captain

parts.note: a roo, short for kangaroo, is an animal that bounces along

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of the word tests is taken

explanation.surface: Cricket talk: a short-pitched ball tests the England skipper at the start of his innings.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface a bouncer is a cricket delivery; in the wordplay it is a kangaroo.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Root, the batsman, captained England's Test cricket team when this puzzle appeared.

clue.text: A big hand from capacity audience

definitions.meaning: in poker, three of a kind plus a pair is a strong holding
a theatre with every seat sold has this, and may hang up a sign saying so

explanation.surface: A theatre crowd that fills every seat gives a performer a great round of applause.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both the poker hand of three of a kind with a pair and a theatre filled to capacity.

clue.text: Yankee vice ring infiltrated somewhere in Somerset

parts.note: Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: infiltrated means the ring has got inside the word for vice

parts.note: vice, wickedness, is evil
a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: An American crime ring has been infiltrated somewhere in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'ring' a criminal gang; it is just the letter O, which 'infiltrated' puts into EVIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeovil is a market town in the English county of Somerset, so it is an example of a place there.

clue.text: Beat back rookie grabbing learner driver, maybe

indicators.note: back means the word for beat is read in reverse

parts.note: to beat someone is to flog them

indicators.note: grabbing means the novice holds the learner letter inside it

parts.note: a cub is a novice, as in a cub reporter
L is the learner sign on British cars

explanation.surface: A rookie driving instructor beats a retreat, grabbing a learner driver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'driver, maybe' looks like the learner at the wheel; it is the definition, a club used on the golf course. 'back' and 'grabbing' are the indicators.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver is one example of the sticks golfers swing, the long-hitting wood used off the tee.

clue.text: Plucky lot with rival finish on court

parts.note: a game person is plucky, willing to have a go
a lot or a set is a group of things
and is the word meaning together with
to match someone is to rival them

explanation.surface: A brave team joins a rival at the end of a game on court.
explanation.definitionFit: The umpire's call at the conclusion of a tennis match announces that the winner has taken it.

clue.text: Learned Lima route overlooking home

parts.note: Lima is L in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: overlooking means missing out, so the word for home is dropped from the route

parts.note: an itinerary is a planned route
in means at home

explanation.surface: An educated traveller's route through Lima skips home altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooking' looks like a view over home; it means leaving out IN, so ITINERARY loses IN to give ITERARY.
explanation.definitionFit: Learned writing or people are bookish, devoted to scholarship and the written word.

clue.text: Dance company never gets awards at first

indicators.note: at first means only the opening letters of never, gets and awards are used

explanation.surface: A dance troupe complains it never wins any prizes at the outset.
explanation.definitionFit: The conga is a Latin American dance done in a long single-file line.

clue.text: Fluky piece finished around noon

indicators.note: around means the joined words go round the noon letter

parts.note: a unit is a single piece of something
finished means ended

explanation.surface: A lucky bit of work was completed at about midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts N into UNITENDED, between UNI and TENDED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fluky happens by chance, not by design, so it was never planned.

clue.text: Share memory about old pots here

parts.note: to pool resources is to share them

indicators.note: about means the memory letters go round the old letter

parts.note: ROM is read-only memory in computing

explanation.surface: Someone recalls sharing out old pots, maybe at a pottery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pots' suggests ceramics, but it is the verb: players pot balls in billiards and snooker.
explanation.definitionFit: A billiard hall is where balls get sunk into pockets, a room for cue games.

clue.text: Offence beside goal reflected game

indicators.note: reflected, as in a mirror, means the joined words are read right to left

parts.note: an offence against morality is a sin
net is a goal, as in to find the net

explanation.surface: A footballer, fouling near the goalmouth, thinks again about the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflected' reverses SINNET.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn tennis is a racket sport, one example of a competitive pastime.

clue.text: After renovation, their bars had a very tight margin …

indicators.note: after renovation suggests something rebuilt, so the letters of their bars had are rearranged

explanation.surface: Once refurbished, the pubs' bars only just squeaked through.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning by the width of a single hair is the narrowest of escapes.

clue.text: Article describes excellent case for sport

indicators.note: describes means draws a line round, so the word for article goes round the other two

parts.note: an article is an object, a thing
A1 means excellent, read here as AI
a box is a case or container

explanation.surface: A newspaper article sets out a strong legal case for some sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describes' is used in its geometric sense of drawing a line round something. A1, first-rate, is written with the letter I in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Muay Thai, the kickboxing martial art of Thailand, is a combat sport.

clue.text: … such as this second person once

definitions.meaning: continuing the previous clue, a tiny margin of one thousandth of an inch is an example
the old singular form of you, used in the Bible and Shakespeare

explanation.definitionFit: Engineers call a thousandth of an inch this, and archaic English used it for the singular you.

clue.text: Staggering growth in illegal delivery style at Lord's

indicators.note: staggering means reeling unsteadily, so the letters of growth in are mixed up

explanation.surface: Commentators note amazing growth in a banned bowling action.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is London's famous cricket ground. 'Staggering' looks like 'astonishing'; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a bowler who straightens the elbow is chucking, which is against the laws and gets called no-ball.

clue.text: Endless battle to accommodate river sport

indicators.note: to accommodate means the shortened battle holds the river inside it
endless means the final letter of the battle is cut off

parts.note: Waterloo, 1815, was Napoleon's final battle
the Po is Italy's longest river

explanation.surface: A never-ending fight to house a river sounds like a sporting contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' drops the battle's final letter and 'to accommodate' holds the river inside what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A team game played by swimmers in a pool, passing a ball into goals at each end.

clue.text: English medic and old PM almost ready for fight

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the old premier's name is dropped

parts.note: Clement Attlee was British prime minister from 1945 to 1951

explanation.surface: An English doctor and a former prime minister are nearly geared up for battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims ATTLEE to ATTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To embattle troops is to draw them up in battle array, preparing them for combat.

clue.text: Official who's often up the pole?

definitions.text: Official who's often up the pole?

parts.words: Official who's often up the pole?
parts.note: a referee's assistant runs the touchline with a flag on a pole, and a worker on overhead cables climbs telegraph poles

explanation.walkthrough: The flag held aloft and the climbing cable worker share the name; 'up the pole' is also slang for mistaken, as officials are often thought to be.
explanation.definitionFit: A football or tennis official watching the lines, and a utility worker who repairs overhead lines.

clue.text: Current ball supporters

definitions.meaning: a current is a flowing stream, here the river in north-east England
golfers rest the ball on small pegs before driving

explanation.definitionFit: The River Tees flows through Middlesbrough, and golf pegs that hold the ball up share its name.

clue.text: Cousins did this well, working at desk

indicators.note: working means set in motion, so the letters of at desk are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some cousins did well in their office jobs, working at a desk.
explanation.walkthrough: Cousins is Robin Cousins, the British figure skater who won Olympic gold in 1980, not a relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure skater glided over ice, which is what the champion did so successfully.

clue.text: Pongy during hard slog, one's taking time off

indicators.note: during means the smelly word sits within the punch

parts.note: a haymaker is a wild swinging punch, a slog
olid is an old word for smelly, which is what pongy means in British slang

explanation.surface: Something smells during hard graft, and someone wants a break from work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard slog' looks like toil; it is a wild punch. 'during' places the smelly word inside it, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tourist on vacation is a person enjoying a break from work.

clue.text: Snowman? College erected it

indicators.note: erected means put up, so in a down answer the word for college is read bottom to top

parts.note: uni is short for university, a college

explanation.surface: Students at a college built a snowman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erected' reverses UNI as it is read upwards in a down entry. The question mark warns that 'Snowman' is a playful description.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Arctic peoples of Canada and Greenland, a land of snow and ice.

clue.text: Yell for one during tennis lesson

indicators.note: during means the letters are found running inside tennis lesson

explanation.surface: A coach shouts at a pupil in the middle of a tennis lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yell' is not a shout but one of the Shetland Islands, north of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Yell is an example of an island, the second largest in the Shetland group.

clue.text: Card game to stimulate tense F1 driver

parts.note: to pique interest is to stimulate it
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Playing cards to provoke a nervous racing driver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'F1 driver' is a second definition: Nelson Piquet was a three-time Formula One world champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Piquet is an old two-player card game played with a 32-card pack.

clue.text: It most often primarily takes suet that's put out

definitions.text: It most often primarily takes suet that's put out

indicators.note: put out means disordered, so the letters are rearranged
primarily means only the first letters of most and often are used

explanation.surface: Garden birdwatching: one particular bird is usually first to the suet left out on a feeder.
explanation.walkthrough: IT plus M and O (from 'most often primarily') plus SUET are rearranged by 'put out'. The whole clue also describes the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: This small bird, a tit, is a regular visitor to garden feeders where fat and suet are hung out.

clue.text: Young openers show energy and horsepower

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for energy in physics
split as horse and power: a gee-gee, GG, is a horse in nursery language, and teeth means power, as in a law with teeth

explanation.surface: Junior opening batsmen display vigour and great strength.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'horsepower' as two words: horse (GG) and power (TEETH). The 'openers' are tools for breaking out of eggshells, not batsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: Hatchling birds and reptiles use a small hard tip on the beak or snout to break open the shell.

clue.text: Cook finished batter

parts.note: to do food is to cook it, as in done to a turn
over means finished, as in the game is over

explanation.surface: A chef has completed the batter mix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'batter' looks like the cook's mixture; it is the verb meaning beat up.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone over is British slang for giving them a beating, so it means assault.
